body: 1995 letter: 'In business, I look for economic castles protected by unbreachable "moats."' (GEICO's moat widened as expenses fell to 23.6% of premiums). 1996: GEICO's 'economies of scale ... should allow us to maintain or even widen the protective moat'; its 'sustainable cost advantage' is what attracted him in 1951. 1987 letter on unglamorous holdings: 'Severe change and exceptional returns usually don't mix. Most investors, of course, behave as if just the opposite were true', conferring 'the highest price-earnings ratios on exotic-sounding businesses that hold out the promise of feverish change.' And: 'a business that constantly encounters major change also encounters many chances for major error ... economic terrain that is forever shifting violently is ground on which it is difficult to build a fortress-like business franchise. Such a franchise is usually the key to sustained high returns.' 1989 acquisition criteria: 'demonstrated consistent earning power (future projections are of little interest to us, nor are "turnaround" situations)', good ROE with little debt, 'simple businesses (if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it)'. Actionable: weight 'stable industry + widening cost or brand advantage' over 'disruption story'; check whether the moat is widening (falling unit cost vs peers, rising share) each year rather than assuming it.

data.moat_test: unit cost or brand advantage widening year by year

title: Buffett 1987/1995: castles with moats; 'Severe change and exceptional returns usually don't mix'
